d: Annual fee paid to the manager to run the fund, usually charged quarterly in advance. It pays salaries, offices and operations, and should not be the main source of profit for the GP.
x: 2% a year in VC; 1.5–2% in mid-market PE.
1% on invested capital for a large private credit fund.
s: A €100m fund at 2% charges €2m a year for five years, then steps down.
Over ten years fees can total 15–20% of commitments, which is why fee basis and step-downs matter.
The fund holds first close late in the year.
Fees accrue from first close; later LPs pay equalised fees back to that date.

d: What the fee percentage is charged on: committed capital during the investment period, then usually invested capital, meaning the cost of investments still held, net of write-offs.
x: 2% of commitments in years 1–5, then 2% of invested capital.
A credit fund charging on NAV.
s: A company is written off in year 6.
Its cost leaves the invested-capital base, so fees fall.
Fees on NAV during a boom.
Fees rise with marks, rewarding valuations rather than exits; LPs prefer cost basis.

d: A cut in the fee rate or base after the investment period ends or a successor fund starts charging fees.
x: 2% on commitments, then 1.5% on invested capital.
Fee halved once Fund II begins charging.
s: Fund II launches in year 4.
Fund I fees step down early, avoiding double fees for the same team time.
No step-down in the LPA.
LPs push for one at the next fund.

d: A management fee set from an agreed operating budget rather than a fixed percentage, so fee income tracks real costs. Favoured by some large LPs for big funds.
x: Fee set annually from a budget agreed with the LPAC.
A sovereign fund SMA paying actual costs plus a margin.
s: The manager's costs fall after deployment.
The fee falls with them, unlike a fixed 2%.
Budget overruns.
The manager absorbs costs above the agreed budget.

d: Reductions in the management fee for LPs that commit early or commit large amounts. Common tools to build first-close momentum.
x: 0.25% off the fee for LPs in first close.
1.5% fee for commitments over €50m instead of 2%.
s: Later LPs ask for the early-close discount via MFN.
Timing-based discounts are usually excluded from MFN.
Too many discounts.
Fee income may fall below the ManCo budget.

d: Fees portfolio companies pay the manager for arranging deals, sitting on boards or providing services. Increasingly offset against the management fee.
x: A 1% transaction fee on a buyout.
Annual monitoring fees from portfolio companies.
s: The manager earns €2m of deal fees.
With a 100% offset, LP management fees fall by €2m.
Monitoring fees accelerate on exit.
LPs scrutinise these; ILPA templates require disclosure.

d: The share of transaction and monitoring fees credited against the management fee. Institutional LPs now expect 100%.
x: 100% offset of all portfolio company fees.
80% offset in an older fund.
s: Offsets exceed fees in a quarter.
Excess carries forward to future quarters.
Operating partner fees are excluded from offset.
LPs negotiate whether they count.

d: Costs of setting up the fund (legal, regulatory, fundraising travel) charged to the fund up to a cap. The manager pays anything above it.
x: Cap of 0.5–1% of commitments.
€1m cap on a €200m fund.
s: Legal fees reach €1.4m against a €1m cap.
The manager pays €400k.
Placement fees counted as organisational expenses.
Usually excluded or offset.

d: Running costs the fund bears directly: audit, administration, depositary, deal costs, insurance. The LPA lists what the manager must pay itself.
x: Annual fund expenses of 0.3% of commitments.
Broken-deal and legal costs charged to the fund.
s: The manager charges compliance staff costs to the fund.
LPs object if the LPA treats them as manager overhead.
Expenses spike in a year.
LPs review against the expense cap if any.

d: A limit on annual fund expenses or specific categories, with the manager bearing any excess. Common in smaller funds and evergreen products.
x: Fund expenses capped at 0.5% of NAV per year.
A cap on investor reporting costs.
s: Expenses exceed the cap.
The manager reimburses the excess.
A large litigation cost arises.
Many caps exclude extraordinary items.

d: Costs of deals that did not complete, such as legal and diligence fees. Usually borne by the fund and shared with co-investors pro rata.
x: €300k of diligence on a failed buyout.
Broken-deal costs allocated to co-investors.
s: Co-investors pay nothing.
The fund bears all costs; LPs push for pro rata sharing.
A deal breaks due to GP error.
LPs may argue the manager should bear it.

d: The GP's share of the fund's profits, paid only once LPs have their capital back and any hurdle. Standard rate is 20%; some top VC firms charge 25–30%.
x: On €150m of profit at 20% carry the GP receives €30m.
Carry held by partners through a separate carry vehicle.
s: The fund returns exactly its capital.
No profit, no carry.
A partner leaves in year 3.
Unvested carry is forfeited under the vesting schedule.

d: Carry rates that step up with performance, for example 20% up to 3x and 25% above. Rewards outperformance without raising the base rate.
x: 20% carry below 2.5x net, 30% above.
A VC fund with 25% above 3x TVPI.
s: The fund reaches 3.2x.
The higher rate applies to profits above the tier.
LPs worry about risk-seeking.
Tiers based on net multiple reduce incentives to chase IRR.

d: How the GP's carry is divided among partners and staff, usually set in the carry vehicle's documents, with vesting and leaver rules.
x: 60% to founding partners, 40% to the wider team.
Points allocated per person with annual vesting.
s: A new partner joins in year 3.
They receive points from an unallocated reserve or by dilution.
A good leaver departs.
They keep vested points; unvested points return to the pool.

d: The minimum return LPs must receive before the GP earns carry, usually 8% a year compounded on contributed capital. Many VC funds have no hurdle.
x: 8% compounded annual hurdle in buyout funds.
A credit fund with a 6% hurdle.
s: The fund returns 7% a year.
Below the hurdle, so no carry is earned.
Simple vs compound hurdle.
Compounding increases the amount LPs receive first; LPAs specify which.

d: A hurdle with no GP catch-up: the GP earns carry only on profits above the hurdle, not on all profits. Rare in PE, more common in some real estate and hedge structures.
x: 20% carry only on returns above 8%.
A real estate fund with a hard 7% hurdle.
s: Profit is 10% a year.
Carry applies to the 2% above the hurdle only.
Comparing to a soft hurdle.
Soft hurdles with catch-up give the GP 20% of all profit once cleared.

d: After LPs reach the hurdle, the GP receives all or most of the next distributions until it has its full carry share of total profit. With a full catch-up, the hurdle changes when carry is paid but not the final split.
x: 100% catch-up until the GP has 20% of profits.
80% catch-up (GP takes 80%, LPs 20%) until caught up.
s: Proceeds just clear the hurdle.
The catch-up starts; the GP's share rises quickly.
Partial catch-up.
The GP reaches 20% more slowly; LPs keep more along the way.

d: The order in which proceeds are paid: return of capital, preferred return, GP catch-up, then the carry split.
x: A four-tier European waterfall.
An American deal-by-deal waterfall with loss carryforward.
s: A €250m distribution on €100m paid-in.
Tiers pay LPs €100m, then pref, then GP catch-up, then 80/20.
Administrator and GP models differ.
They reconcile before payment.

d: Whole-fund waterfall. The GP earns carry only after LPs have received all contributed capital across the whole fund, plus the preferred return. Standard in Europe and preferred by LPs.
x: Carry paid only after cumulative distributions exceed paid-in plus 8%.
A Luxembourg fund using the ILPA whole-of-fund model.
s: An early exit returns 5x on one deal.
No carry yet if total distributions are below paid-in plus pref.
The GP wants earlier carry.
LPs may accept interim carry with escrow.

d: Deal-by-deal waterfall. Carry is paid on each realised investment, usually after returning capital for that deal and covering realised losses. The GP is paid earlier, so clawback matters more.
x: Carry on each exit after returning that deal's cost plus realised losses.
A US buyout fund with deal-by-deal carry and 30% escrow.
s: Early winners, later losers.
The GP may have taken too much carry; clawback applies at the end.
LPs negotiate protections.
Escrow, interim clawback and GP guarantees.

d: First tier of the waterfall: distributions go 100% to LPs until they have received back everything they contributed, including fees and expenses.
x: €100m paid-in returned before any pref.
Return of capital including fees in a European waterfall.
s: Only invested capital is returned first.
LPs prefer all contributions, including fees.
A partial return.
Remaining capital is returned from later proceeds.

d: The GP's obligation to return carry if, at the end of the fund, it has received more than its agreed share of total profit. Usually capped at the after-tax amount received.
x: €4m returned by the GP after late write-offs.
Clawback tested at the end of the fund and on interim dates.
s: The GP has distributed carry to partners who left.
Recovery may depend on individual guarantees.
Clawback capped after tax.
LPs recover less than the excess carry.

d: Clawback tested before the end of the fund, for example annually or at end of investment period, so excess carry is returned sooner.
x: Annual clawback test in a deal-by-deal fund.
Clawback test at year 7.
s: Losses appear in year 6.
Interim clawback returns excess carry then, not in year 12.
GP resists.
LPs may trade interim clawback for a larger escrow.

d: Personal guarantees from carry recipients (individually, often several not joint) or a parent company guarantee securing the GP's clawback obligation.
x: Partners guaranteeing their pro rata share of clawback.
A parent guarantee from a listed asset manager.
s: The GP entity has no assets.
Guarantees let LPs recover from individuals.
Several, not joint.
Each partner owes only their share.

d: Part of each carry payment held back in an account to secure a possible clawback.
x: 30% of carry held in escrow until wind-up.
Escrow released once the fund passes 1.5x.
s: Clawback arises.
Escrowed amounts are applied first.
Escrow earns interest.
The LPA says who receives it.

d: The schedule over which team members earn their allocation of carry, so that leavers forfeit the unvested part.
x: Vesting over five years with a one-year cliff.
Bad leavers forfeiting all carry.
s: A partner leaves in year 2 of 5.
40% vested; 60% returns to the pool.
A partner is dismissed for cause.
Bad leaver provisions may cancel vested carry too.

d: The GP gives up part of its fee in exchange for an extra profit share in the fund. Used for tax reasons in some countries; SEBI does not accept it toward continuing interest.
x: A GP waiving €1m of fees for a priority profit share.
Waiver used to fund GP commitment.
s: Tax authority challenges the waiver.
Rules vary; some treat waived fees as income.
LPs ask for cash GP commitment instead.
Common LP preference.

d: The fair value of the fund's remaining investments plus cash, minus liabilities. Reported quarterly under the valuation policy.
x: NAV of €140m on €100m paid-in.
NAV per unit for an open-ended fund.
s: NAV rises after a round at a higher price.
It is a paper gain until exit.
Stale NAVs in a falling market.
Secondary buyers discount them.

a: internal rate of return, money-weighted return
d: Internal rate of return: the annual discount rate at which the present value of all cash flows is zero. It rewards speed, so early exits and subscription lines push it up, and it says nothing about the amount of money made.
x: A 25% IRR from a 2x return in three years.
An 18% IRR from 3x over seven years.
s: One quick flip produces 80% IRR.
Fund IRR jumps even though little money was made.
IRR used for comparison.
Pair it with multiples and PME.

d: IRR on the fund's investments themselves, before management fees, fund expenses and carried interest. It shows the manager's deal-level skill; LPs care about net IRR, and the gap between the two is the gross-to-net spread.
x: Gross IRR of 28% on realised deals.
Gross IRR shown deal by deal in a track record.
s: Marketing shows only gross IRR.
SEC Marketing Rule requires net alongside gross for registered advisers.
Comparing gross across managers.
Fees differ, so net is the fair comparison.

d: IRR from the LP's side, after fees, expenses and carry. The figure LPs compare across funds.
x: Net IRR of 19% vs gross 26%.
Net IRR computed on LP cash flows.
s: A fund's net IRR falls late in life.
Fees continue while gains slow.
LPs compute net IRR from their own cash flows.
It may differ slightly from the fund-level figure due to timing.

d: An IRR that assumes distributions are reinvested at a chosen rate and contributions financed at another, reducing IRR's bias toward early winners.
x: MIRR of 15% vs IRR of 22% assuming 8% reinvestment.
MIRR used by an LP to compare funds.
s: A fund with early exits shows very high IRR.
MIRR shows a lower, more realistic figure.
Choosing the reinvestment rate.
Results depend on it; disclose the assumption.

d: A return measure that removes the effect of cash flow timing, used for open-ended and listed funds where the manager does not control contributions.
x: Quarterly TWR for an evergreen fund.
Comparing an open-ended fund to an index.
s: Comparing a closed-end fund using TWR.
Not appropriate; the GP controls timing, so IRR fits better.
Evergreen fund marketing.
TWR is the norm.

d: Total value to paid-in: distributions plus NAV, divided by paid-in capital. TVPI = DPI + RVPI.
x: 1.8x means €1.80 of value for every euro paid in.
TVPI of 3.0x for a top-quartile VC fund.
s: TVPI of 2.5x but DPI of 0.3x.
Most value is unrealised and depends on future exits.
TVPI falls after a down round.
Marks change; realised value does not.

d: Distributions to paid-in: cash returned divided by capital contributed. The only part of performance that is realised.
x: DPI of 1.2x means LPs have their money back plus 20%.
DPI of 0.1x in year 5.
s: LPs focus on DPI in a slow exit market.
Funds with high TVPI but low DPI struggle to raise.
NAV loans used to boost DPI.
LPs look at the source of distributions.

d: Residual value to paid-in: current NAV divided by capital paid in. It is the unrealised part of TVPI (TVPI = DPI + RVPI). A high RVPI late in a fund's life means most of the value is still a valuation, not cash returned.
x: RVPI of 1.4x in year 6.
RVPI falling as exits occur.
s: RVPI high late in life.
Exit risk remains; secondaries may price at a discount.
RVPI drops after write-offs.
TVPI falls.

a: multiple on invested capital, gross multiple
d: Multiple on invested capital: value of an investment, realised plus unrealised, divided by its cost. Usually quoted gross at deal level.
x: A 4x MOIC on a €5m investment.
Fund-level gross MOIC of 2.4x.
s: High MOIC but slow.
IRR may be modest; both matter.
MOIC vs TVPI.
MOIC is gross on invested capital; TVPI is net on paid-in.

d: Public market equivalent: compares the fund with an index by running the fund's own cash flows through the index. A Kaplan-Schoar PME above 1.0 means the fund beat the market.
x: KS-PME of 1.3 against the MSCI World.
PME used in LP investment committee papers.
s: A fund shows 15% IRR when the index rose 20% a year.
PME below 1 shows it lagged.
Choosing the index.
The benchmark should match risk and geography.

d: An annualised measure of excess return over a public index, derived from PME methods, expressing outperformance as a rate rather than a ratio.
x: Direct alpha of 4% a year over the S&P 500.
Used alongside KS-PME in academic studies.
s: LP wants an annual outperformance figure.
Direct alpha gives a rate comparable to IRR.
Negative direct alpha.
The fund underperformed the index.

d: The pattern of negative returns in a fund's early years, from fees, costs and cautious valuations, followed by gains as investments mature and exit.
x: Net IRR of −12% in year 2, +18% by year 8.
A secondary fund buying later to avoid the J-curve.
s: An LP panics at year-2 losses.
The J-curve is expected; judge funds later.
Sub lines shallow the J-curve.
They delay calls, improving early IRR.

d: The year a fund made its first investment or held first close. Funds are benchmarked against others of the same vintage.
x: A 2021 vintage VC fund.
Comparing 2015 and 2016 vintages.
s: 2021 vintages face low marks.
Benchmarks show peers suffered too.
A fund chooses its vintage definition.
Consistency matters; LPs check.

d: Where a fund sits against peers of the same vintage and strategy in a benchmark dataset. Top-quartile claims depend heavily on which dataset and metric are used.
x: Top quartile by net IRR in one dataset, second by TVPI in another.
A fund citing Cambridge Associates benchmarks.
s: Many GPs claim top quartile.
LPs check dataset, metric and date.
Quartile changes over time.
Early rankings are unreliable.

a: Cambridge Associates, MSCI Burgiss, Preqin, PitchBook
d: Firms that collect fund cash flows and NAVs to publish peer benchmarks. Datasets differ by coverage and source (LP-reported vs GP-reported), so the same fund can rank differently.
x: Cambridge Associates' US PE benchmark.
MSCI Burgiss LP-sourced data.
s: A GP picks the dataset that ranks it best.
LPs ask for rankings across sources.
Indian AIFs.
SEBI requires performance benchmarking through approved agencies.

d: The spread between top and bottom funds. It is wide in VC and buyout and narrow in core real estate and credit, which is why manager selection matters most in VC.
x: Top-quartile VC at 3x vs bottom at 0.8x.
Senior credit funds clustered within a few points.
s: An LP builds a VC programme.
It spends more on manager selection because dispersion is high.
Credit allocation.
Lower dispersion means fees and costs matter more.

d: Whether a manager's past outperformance predicts future results. Studies found persistence in VC and weaker persistence in buyout in recent decades.
x: A VC firm with three top-quartile funds in a row.
Buyout manager reverting to median.
s: An LP re-ups only on past returns.
Persistence is imperfect; diligence team and strategy too.
Fund II raised before Fund I results are clear.
LPs rely on early marks with caution.

d: The share of investments returning more than cost. In VC low hit rates are normal because a few winners drive returns.
x: 40% of deals above 1x in a VC fund.
80% hit rate in a buyout fund.
s: A VC fund has a 30% hit rate but 3x net.
Normal given power law outcomes.
A buyout fund with 50% hit rate.
Signals problems; buyout relies on fewer losses.

d: The gap between gross and net returns caused by management fees, fund expenses and carried interest. For a typical buyout fund it runs at several percentage points of IRR; LPs compare it across managers to judge what the fee terms really cost.
x: Gross 25%, net 18%.
Gross 3.0x, net 2.4x.
s: Spread widens in a small fund.
Fixed costs weigh more.
LP negotiates lower fees.
The spread narrows.

d: Share of invested capital that went into deals returned at less than cost. It shows how often a manager loses money and how badly; buyout funds aim for a low loss ratio, while venture funds accept a high one in exchange for a few outsized winners.
x: 25% loss ratio in a VC fund.
5% loss ratio in a buyout fund.
s: A high loss ratio.
The fund needs bigger winners to compensate.
Loss ratio by cost vs count.
Report both.

d: A breakdown of a deal's return into revenue growth, margin improvement, multiple expansion and leverage. LPs use it to see whether returns came from operations or market tailwinds.
x: A buyout return: 50% revenue growth, 20% margin, 30% multiple expansion.
A bridge showing leverage paydown.
s: Returns came mostly from multiple expansion.
LPs question repeatability.
Operational gains dominate.
Supports the GP's value creation claims.

d: Realised value is cash or listed shares already distributed; unrealised value is NAV still held. A track record heavy in unrealised value is less certain.
x: €80m realised and €120m unrealised.
Track record split into realised and unrealised deals.
s: A Fund II raise with Fund I mostly unrealised.
LPs discount marks.
Partial realisations.
Show them separately.
